calibration.note: Realized win rate vs the confidence you STATED at entry, by bucket. A large negative calibration_gap_pct means your confidence is inflated; cap stated confidence until the gap closes (per the Learning Protocol).

target_calibration.note: Grades the claim behind min_risk_reward_ratio. Targets stay NON-BINDING for exits (letting winners run is correct); this measures whether the claimed RR was ever real. rr_inflation is WITHHELD until the sample binds.

Weekly self-review: Last Friday's (7/31) stated change was to explicitly ask, whenever a watchlist name's would_buy_at condition was met or nearly met and still wasn't bought, whether the fat-pitch bar itself is set too high for this account's stated purpose. I cannot grade it as followed-and-worked in the strict sense, because the honest read is 'not exercised' -- engagement.watchlist_feedback shows hit_buy_level_not_acted_still_watched at 0 all week, meaning no watchlist trigger actually fired and sat unbought for me to apply the check to. The two biggest watchlist movers this week, TEAM (+51.9%) and SNOW (+26.4%), both moved without ever reaching their stated levels (TEAM's whole move was today's 8/7 earnings gap; SNOW stayed priced at 146x forward earnings) -- extension, not a missed trigger, so the specific mechanism the change targeted never came up. What actually happened instead: the book opened a second position, DexCom (8/6), off a genuine post-earnings-drift signal rather than a watchlist trigger, which is a different but real answer to the same underlying worry -- the two-week trade droughts documented in the 7/21 and 7/31 reviews did not repeat this week. Track record is unchanged: still 2 closed trades (DELL -13.52, HPE -4.53), both from mid-July, anecdote-phase calibration -- BKR and DXCM are both still open, so there's no new win/loss evidence yet on whether this week's picks were actually good. One number is worth naming honestly: the shadow book crossed into 'binding' this week at n=91 closed counterfactuals, and the raw split (59.3% regret_miss vs 39.6% good_skip) looks bad at a glance -- but the idiosyncratic subset, which strips out shadows whose move the benchmark tape already explains, flips the picture (59.5% good_skip vs 37.8% regret among n=37 idiosyncratic cases). Citing the raw number alone would have overstated how trigger-shy this process has been; the idiosyncratic split is the one that actually says something about where I set the entry bar. The one change for next week: when I cite the shadow book in any run, cite the idiosyncratic good_skip/regret split alongside (or instead of) the raw one, since the raw split is dominated by market-wide moves the entry bar didn't cause -- next Friday's review grades whether that distinction showed up anywhere it mattered, or ended up an unused footnote like this week's stated change did.
